title: Sold for a few coins
hookLine: a caravan pulls him out and sells him cheaply in Egypt
carry: the price they paid isn't your worth

cards: A caravan of travelers comes by the well. They send their water-drawer, and he lets down his bucket. It comes up heavy.
He looks in and shouts: good news! Here's a boy! For a boy who's been waiting in the dark, that sounds like rescue.
Except the men up top aren't rescuers. They're traders. And a boy, to a trader, is something else.

teach.b: Surah Yusuf. They hid him away as merchandise, and sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams, counted out.
The Arabic for that price is bakhs, a cheated, short-changed price, less than a thing is worth. And the verse adds: they thought little of him.
The boy who dreamed the stars bowing, sold for pocket change by men who didn't much care.

Commentators have noted that a price you can count, a few coins rather than a weighed amount, was itself a sign of how cheap it was. Now watch the next verse, because the Qur'an turns the whole scene around.
The man in Egypt who bought him says to his wife: make his stay honorable. Perhaps he'll be of use to us, or we might take him as a son. Sound familiar?
It should. Two weeks ago, in Pharaoh's palace, Pharaoh's wife, the woman tradition calls Asiya, looked at baby Musa and said almost the same words.
Two boys, in two stories, taken into an Egyptian house by someone who saw what the world had missed.
Then the verse says: and so We established Yusuf in the land, and Allah is in full command of His affairs, but most people don't know.
The traders set the price. They didn't set his worth. The boy they sold for a handful of coins is, in the story's own words, being established.
Nobody watching that sale could have guessed it.

how: Muslim teachers draw from Yusuf's sale the lesson that human judgments of worth are not Allah's, and point to 12:21, which says Allah is in full command of His affairs, though most people don't know it.

o: a fair price agreed by both buyer and seller
the caravan's tax for crossing into Egypt
a cheated price, far less than a thing is worth

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: sold him for a few coins

s: the caravan rescued Yusuf and took him home
they hid him as merchandise and sold him cheaply in Egypt.
the man who bought Yusuf used almost the same words as Pharaoh's wife
perhaps he'll be of use to us, or we might take him as a son.
the Qur'an says the traders valued Yusuf highly
it says they thought little of him.

games.q: you're the caravan's water-drawer. you let your bucket down the well and it comes up with a boy in it. what do you shout?
games.why: good news! here's a boy! but it was good news for a trader: they hid him as goods and sold him for a few coins.

practice: Think of a time someone set a low price on you: passed over for the job, talked over in the meeting, treated like you were extra in your own family.
Then gently separate two things, what they paid or thought or offered, and what you actually are, and say it to yourself slowly: that was their price, not my worth.
If you pray, you can remember how the verse ends: Allah is in full command of His affairs.

wordCard.voice: Bakhs, a cheated price: what the traders paid for Yusuf, thinking little of him, while Allah was establishing him in the land.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 12:20: a paltry, short-changed price — less than the thing is worth.

carryVoice: Your line: the price they paid isn't your worth. The buyer in Egypt saw what the traders missed. Fifty-nine, and counting.
